title: Free build week one: pitch, plan, price
summary: The person is named and the pick is yours: sketch three ideas, choose one, draw the plan, and price every part against the cap, with the pay yourself first slice set aside before the shopping list starts.
materials: the free build idea page with the circled name
seven stiff card strips and paper fasteners or tape, for the science moment
laptop and a grown-up, for hunting real prices

steps.body: Five minutes on your typing site, home row first, eyes on the screen. Then this week's words, ten times each, fast and without looking down: plan, parts, price, total, budget, cap. Finish by typing the sentence that runs the whole week, twice, no looking: Pay yourself first, then price the rest.

steps.title: Ask, imagine, plan, for a real person
steps.body:
The design loop, one more time: ask, imagine, plan, build, test, fix. Every build this season ran the loop for you. This one runs it for someone else, the person whose name you circled at the showcase, and that changes the ask: not can I build it, but will it actually help them?

This is your build. You pick the problem and you pick the fix. The family gets exactly one lever this week, and it comes at the pitch: they may cross-examine your budget line by line, and they may never argue with your choice. That deal cuts both ways, so honour your side of it: the money has to be real, every line of it.

The week has three jobs, and they land in order. Imagine: three different sketches for the person's problem, because your first idea is rarely your best one, it is just your first. Choose and plan: one sketch wins, and becomes a real drawing with parts and sizes. Price: every part gets a real price from a real place, the total meets the cap, and before a single part goes on the shopping list, you pay yourself first.

Building starts next week. This week is all thinking on paper, and it is the week that decides whether next week is fun or chaos.

steps.title: Three sketches
steps.body:
Open the idea page and reread what you wrote about your person: their groans, their wishes, the scribbles two showcases piled up since week 1. Copy their best groan to the top of a fresh graph paper page, in their words as close as you can remember.

Now sketch three different fixes for it. Not three versions of one idea, three ideas. For each one: give it a name, draw it rough and quick, write one sentence saying what it does for your person, and circle the part that scares you most, the bit you do not yet know how to make. Every good plan has a scary part; a plan with no scary part is usually a plan you have already built before, wearing a hat.

If the page feels thin, two seeds are on offer from last season's someday list: the step counter and the compass, both micro:bit builds that never got their day. Take a seed only if it truly fits your person's groan. They are offers, not homework.

Sketching rules: ugly drawings are fine, labels beat beauty, and nothing gets crossed out. A bad sketch earns its keep by making the good one obvious.
checklist: The person's groan is written at the top of the page, in their words
Three genuinely different ideas are sketched, each with a name and a one-sentence job
The scariest part of each sketch is circled
At least one sketch scares me a little, and I can say which part and why

steps.title: Choose one and draw the plan
steps.body:
Put the three sketches in front of you and run each through three tests, out loud. Does it truly fix the groan at the top of the page? Can it be built in the two build weeks left, with the tools you have, and still leave room in the second one to test it on your person and fix what they find? And the circled scary part: do you have a first idea for how to attack it, plus a plan B if that idea fails? Score honestly. The winner is the sketch that passes all three, not the prettiest one.

Now turn the winner into a plan on a fresh page. If your build is a physical thing: draw it with the ruler, write real sizes on the drawing in centimeters, and put the protractor on every corner that is not square, the way Think taught you this week; a slanted part drawn at its true angle is a part that will actually fit. If your build is a program or a paper thing, the same rules wear different clothes: draw the screens or pages, and list the steps the thing takes, in order, numbered.

Either way, finish the page with the parts list in two columns: what I already have, and what must be bought. Walk the house before anything lands in the buy column; the have column is where budgets are won.

Last line of the page, copied from your sketch: the scary part, and its plan B. Next to it write the first thing you will try.
checklist: The winner passed all three tests out loud, and I can say why each other sketch lost
The plan has real sizes with the ruler, and measured angles where corners are not square, or numbered steps if the build is a program
Every part sits in a column: already have, or must buy
The scary part is named on the plan, with plan A and plan B beside it

A note explains a triangle's three sides alone lock its corners since stiff card cannot stretch, and that the fix for any wobble is a diagonal brace, not more glue.

items.s: A square leans; a triangle can't
A triangle's sides alone lock its corners;
card can't stretch, so it can't lean
Fix for a wobble: add a diagonal brace, not more glue

steps.title: Why triangles hold their shape
steps.body:
Take four strips of stiff card and pin or tape them loosely corner to corner into a square. Push one corner sideways: the square leans over into a diamond without a fight. Now make a triangle from three strips and push however you like. It will not budge. You can break it, but you cannot lean it.

Here is the why. To change a triangle's shape you would have to change the length of one of its three sides, and stiff card does not stretch. The four-sided frame can lean without any side changing length, so nothing stops it leaning. The triangle is the only shape whose sides alone lock its corners, and in Think this week you met the same fact from the other side: three angles that must always share 180 degrees.

Engineers spend that fact everywhere. Look at a crane, a bridge, a roof truss, a bike frame: triangles, triangles, triangles. When they need a square frame to stay square, they cheat a triangle into it, one diagonal brace across the middle, and suddenly the wobble is gone because the diagonal must stretch for the frame to lean.

Keep this in your pocket for the build weeks: if anything you make wobbles, do not push the joints harder. Add a diagonal. The fix for a wobble is almost never more glue, it is a triangle.

figure.alt: A circle representing a globe with a horizontal equator line at zero degrees latitude, two more latitude lines drawn evenly spaced above and below it, and several longitude lines drawn converging toward the top and bottom of the circle. A note explains latitude covers about 111 kilometres per degree everywhere, while longitude lines squeeze together and meet at the poles.

items.s: Latitude and longitude on a sphere
Longitude lines squeeze together and meet at the poles;

steps.title: The grid that wraps around a sphere
steps.body:
Your plan sits on graph paper, a flat grid where every square is the same size. Wrap that idea around a ball and you get latitude and longitude, the grid that pins down any place on Earth.

Latitude counts degrees north or south of the equator. Every one of those degrees measures almost exactly the same distance everywhere on the planet: about 111 kilometres.

Longitude counts degrees east or west, but its lines are not evenly spaced. They sit 111 kilometres apart at the equator and squeeze closer the further you travel, meeting exactly at the poles. A degree of longitude in Alaska covers far less ground than a degree of longitude in Ecuador.

That is the one big difference from flat graph paper. On a sphere, one of the two grid directions changes size depending on where you stand. A flat grid never has to make that trade.

steps.title: Price the list: pay yourself first
steps.body:
Ask the family for the cap: the real number of real dollars this build may spend. Write it big at the top of a fresh page.

Now, before one single part gets priced, the move the week is named for: pay yourself first. Decide the slice of the cap that goes to your savings, take it off the top, and write what is left as your spending number. One coin in ten is the classic slice; the family sets the exact deal. The slice is not leftover money you keep if the shopping goes well. It leaves first, which is the whole trick, and the build makes do with the rest. It always can.

Price the buy column against the spending number. With a grown-up, hunt each part where it really sells, a shop you can reach or a site you both trust, and write each line: part, where, price. Round prices up, never down; the store does not round your way. Add the total, put it next to the spending number, and face the verdict.

Over the number? The budget decides, not the wish. Swap a part for a cheaper cousin, cut a decoration, raid the have column harder. Repeat until the total fits. Under the number? Leave the gap as breathing room; week 10 has a way of finding surprise costs. Finish by writing one backup swap at the bottom: the line you would trade for a cheaper way if the family attacks it at the pitch.
checklist: The cap is written at the top, and the pay yourself first slice came off before any pricing
Every buy line has a part, a real place, and a real price, rounded up
The total sits under the spending number, and I can say what I cut or swapped to get there
One backup swap is written at the bottom for the pitch

steps.title: The priced parts list
steps.body:
The currency and the rounding rule, always round up, stay the same for every row. Each part is priced once, since a real price does not need repeating the way a measurement does.

One row per part on the buy list, at least three parts. For each row, write the part's name and its real price in dollars, rounded up.
steps.question: What is the total of the priced parts, and how much room is left under the spending cap?

steps.title: Ready for the pitch
steps.body:
Everything on your desk now feeds Speak: the pitch is this week, plan and priced list in hand, family gathered, budget cross-examined line by line. Nothing gets bought before their yes.

After the yes, the shopping happens this weekend with a grown-up, from your own list, so the parts are sitting on your desk when week 10 opens. If a part turns out to cost more in real life than on paper, that is not a disaster, that is the budget talking: swap or cut on the spot, the same way you did today, and write the change on the list.

One last thing before you close the Maker's Log: reread your plan's scary part and its plan B. That line is the one the family should poke at hardest, and the one a good engineer is proudest to have written down.

steps.title: Show it
steps.prompt: Photos of the three sketches page, the winning plan with its sizes and angles or numbered steps, and the priced list showing the cap, the pay yourself first slice, and the total that fits.
